# voice-tells — shared AI-voice-tells checklist

Consolidated checklist for "this reads like AI wrote it." Extracted from `engineering-writing` and `pz-voice` under mt#3841 after a 2026-08-08 skill-cluster audit found the same tells content diverging across the two skills. This file is now the single source; [`/engineering-writing`](../engineering-writing/SKILL.md) and [`/pz-voice`](../pz-voice/SKILL.md) point here rather than carrying their own copies.

## Genre boundary — two families, two owners

The checklist keeps two families of "sounds like AI" failure separate, because they're diagnosed differently and owned by different skills upstream:

- **§1 Structural tells** — prose-SHAPE defects any writer (human or model) can fall into regardless of what they're claiming: cadence, templating, punctuation, vocabulary. Detected by re-reading the sentence/paragraph/heading shape. Craft-framing owner: [`/engineering-writing`](../engineering-writing/SKILL.md).
- **§2 Voice-stance violations** — register defects specific to writing IN the principal's voice: postures and claims pz-voice structurally refuses, independent of prose shape. Craft-framing owner: [`/pz-voice`](../pz-voice/SKILL.md) §5-6.

The 2026-08-08 discourse-synthesis gap-fill pass found the two axes orthogonal: a draft can fix every structural tell and still violate voice-stance (SaaS hyperbole in perfectly-cadenced prose), or hold correct no-go-register discipline while every paragraph is the same uniform length. Check both.

## 1. Structural tells

_Refreshed 2026-07-24, consolidated 2026-08-08 against the discourse-synthesis §(e) external pass ([Notion](https://app.notion.com/p/3b6937f03cb481828892de5fcc0c0496)). The tell landscape moves fast and splits by model; recheck against current sources (§External evidence below) every quarter or so rather than trusting this list forever._

These are the patterns readers pattern-match as AI writing. Individual instances aren't damning; clustering is the tell.

This section governs ARTIFACT prose. The conversational sibling — turn-end report register in chat — is owned by `communication-contract.mdc §The Tier-1 turn-report contract → How it reads` (mt#3287); its structural tells (beat lead-ins, punch-fragment drum-hits, significance bids) are the chat-surface form of the same disease this checklist catches in documents (mt#2899 is the artifact-surface half).

### Negation-pivot / contrast-reframe — top-tier, cross-vendor

"It's not X. It's Y." / "not X — it's Y" / "X, not Y" chains. Ranked top-tier and cross-vendor as of the 2026-08 pass: Wikipedia's Signs of AI writing names it; [tropes.fyi](http://tropes.fyi) calls it "Negative Parallelism"; Forbes's 2026 AI-writing-tells list carries it as sign #15. Fix: drop the staged strawman — declare the gap, mechanize the failure it produces, implicate — don't set up a contrast just to knock it down.

### Cadence uniformity — the dominant tell

Rhythm gives away more AI writing than any single word choice, and it's the tell that survives every other fix. Researchers call the human contrast **burstiness**: natural variation in sentence length and rhythm across a passage. Low burstiness — flat and repeating — is what gives AI prose away.

Three shapes to check for:

- **Sentence-length clustering.** Most models default to sentences in the ~18-24 word range and repeat that band paragraph after paragraph.
- **Uniform paragraph length.** Paragraphs come out the same size every time, instead of some running long and others landing in a single line.
- **Paragraph ends on a neat bow.** Every paragraph closes with a summary line restating what it just said.

Catch this by reading a section aloud, not by scanning for words.

### Templated / symmetric headings

Identical heading shapes across sibling sections — `[Noun] that [Verb]s.` repeated eight times, every camp getting the same four bullets, every phase the same four fields. Real writing has ragged edges; let each heading match what's actually distinct about its section.

### Title-case formulaic headings

AI-generated prose trends toward abstract, title-cased, formulaic headings ("The Problem," "Key Considerations," "Why This Matters Now"). Human engineering prose trends toward sentence-case, specific, sometimes-opinionated headings ("GitHub is the outlier," "Four questions, not one"). Full heading-heuristic detail (including named-contribution distinctness checks): [`/engineering-writing`](../engineering-writing/SKILL.md) §Section heading heuristics.

### Reveal-signposting

"Here's the part that...", "here's the thing...", "and here's the tell that...", "here's where it gets interesting." Debate-team cadence: promises a payoff, delivers an ordinary point. Cut the windup. State the point.

### Tricolon abuse / rule of three

Three bullets, three adjectives, three parallel clauses, every section. Fine used once; repeated across a piece, it's a signature — same family as negation-pivot above (both ranked top-tier as of the 2026-08 pass).

### Bold lead-ins

`**The thesis.**`-style beat lead-ins opening a paragraph, used repeatedly. Unbold; let the sentence carry its own weight.

### Copula avoidance

`serves as` / `marks` / `features` / `boasts` instead of `is`. AI avoids plain copulas to sound more consequential than the sentence needs.

### Mystic register in abstract prose

A documented LLM drift vocabulary — spiral, recursion, resonance, lattice, harmonics, attractor, emergence, the void, the center — that reads as the "Spiralism" register (Rolling Stone's 2026 reporting documents a subculture built on it, manifestos included). Abstract, visionary prose is maximally exposed. Fix: ground every abstract claim in a named mechanism, a real system, or a dated artifact; break liturgical cadence deliberately (not every section ends on an aphorism); spiral-family vocabulary only where it does precise technical work.

### Em dash: density + burstiness, not absence alone

The 2026 landscape splits by model — GPT-5.1 suppresses em dashes in most contexts, Claude and Gemini still lean on them — so dash absence no longer proves human writing. **Em-dash rate + burstiness is the only methodologically strong Claude-specific marker found in the 2026-08 external pass** (ROC-AUC 0.96 per the cited stylometric research; the [vrid.ai](https://vrid.ai/blog/signs-of-ai-writing) Feb-2026 table claiming the opposite is stale — treat it as superseded). Budget: roughly 1 per 100 words in Minsky-voice copy (per the discourse-synthesis §8 voice-rules addendum); one or two per ~2000 words in general engineering prose is fine on its own terms.

### Vocabulary

`delve`, `leverage`, `utilize` (when `use` works); `crucial`, `pivotal`, `significant`, `key` (as evaluative adjectives without specifics); `robust`, `meticulous`, `comprehensive`; `foster`, `bolster`, `enhance`, `garner`; `underscore`, `showcase`; `tapestry`, `interplay`, abstract `landscape`; `resonate`, `align`; `enduring`, `testament`; `paradigm`, `holistic`, `synergy`.

The word-list scan alone is weak evidence: the 2026-08 pass found a shipped Minsky site clean against the full 2025 list AND Forbes's 2026 wave, and it still read as AI — the instrument that actually caught it was structural (device counts per page: negation-pivot, heading templates, em-dash density), not vocabulary. Don't stop at the word list.

### Phrases

"It's worth noting that...", "It is important to remember...", "At its core...", "Fundamentally,...", "Ultimately,...", "In today's world...", "One might argue...", "As previously mentioned...", "In conclusion..."

### Borrowed phrasings from sibling work

A specific idiom that earned its place in the essay that invented it becomes a tell when it appears verbatim in a second essay by the same author — it signals "imitating a template," not "writing." Full detail and the sibling-phrasing revision pass: [`/engineering-writing`](../engineering-writing/SKILL.md) §AI-voice tells to avoid → Borrowed phrasings from sibling work.

### Other structural tics

Present-participle summary clauses ("..., highlighting its significance"); bulleted lists where prose flows; callout boxes after every section with a "takeaway"; curly quotes mixed with straight quotes.

### Tone tics

No contractions (human writing mixes them — use `don't`, `it's`, `we're`); flat register start to finish; over-qualified statements ("In many cases, it may be the case that..." — cut to `often`); weasel attribution ("Observers have noted..." — name who, or say `we think`).

## 2. Voice-stance violations — pz-voice §6 no-go register

These aren't prose-SHAPE defects — a sentence can be perfectly bursty, ragged-edged, contraction-rich, and still violate the voice's stance. Craft-framing owner: [`/pz-voice`](../pz-voice/SKILL.md) §5 (the operative-ontology stance these violations break) and §9 (the full writing process). The voice refuses, structurally:

- **SaaS hyperbole.** "The future of X." "Transforms your Y." "Supercharges your Z." "From your first agent to your IPO."
- **Exclamation marks.** Once a year, maximum.
- **Hedging without warrant.** "I think," "in my view," "it seems," "perhaps" — used only when genuinely uncertain, never as a politeness move.
- **Marketing affirmation.** "Game-changing!" "Truly revolutionary." "Unparalleled." Not even ironically.
- **Buzzword stacking.** "Synergistic leverage of holistic frameworks." If you can't say it without the buzzwords, you don't have the claim.
- **Empty intensifiers.** "Really," "very," "quite," "extremely," "definitely."
- **Faux humility.** "Just a thought." "Not sure if this is right, but."
- **Inspirational endings.** Paragraphs ending on "and that's beautiful" or "the future is bright" instead of the argument's implication.
- **Apologizing for technicality.** "Don't worry if this sounds complex." The voice presupposes reader literacy.
